newsitem.title: FRANCE: Growth not enough to cut French deficits - auditors.
newsitem.headline: Growth not enough to cut French deficits - auditors.

text.p: Economic growth alone will not be enough to bring down France's budget deficit, the authors of an independent audit of French public finances said on Monday.

Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet, members of the Court of Auditors, said in a report delivered to the new Socialist-led government that France needed far-reaching reforms in the way the state works to prevent a new rise in budget deficits.
The report estimated the 1997 deficit was running at between 3.5 and 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, compared to 3.0 percent initially forecast by the 1997 Finance Act.
It said an improvement in economic growth should help redress some of the imbalances in French public finances.
"But the detailed and painstaking studies we have just carried out...confirm our belief that even a prolonged and steady return of growth...will not be enough to redress public finances," they said.

Whatever judgment one might have on the "American model" of economic liberalism, they said, even the United States after six years of strong growth had used structural reforms to help lower its deficit.
"It is clear to us that the trend remains a problem. The continued reduction in deficits simply from the expected recovery in growth will not be enough, as of 1998," they said.

The question of how much weak economic growth is responsible for high budget deficits is one which is hotly debated on both the left and right in France as the country comes under pressure from its European partners to liberalise its economy and cut down on state intervention.

The auditors noted that previous governments had begun to reverse a trend in pensions and welfare spending through reforms introduced in 1993 and 1995, under former conservative prime ministers Edouard Balladur and Alain Juppe respectively.
"But deep-rooted reforms are lacking as regards the state," the auditors said.
Simple control of public spending was not enough in a country where the role of the state in the economy was one of the biggest among France's main trading partners.
"French public finances are in crisis. The effort made these last few years have contained the symptoms, but have not been enough to prevent an increase in debt," it said.
France's financial difficulties would remain until it acted to improve the efficiency of state intervention and increase productivity, they said.
